posts.title: [next weekly update]
posts.content:
I added a Gamepad 8Vim Demo to the coding projects page. I was able to copy most of the logic from my python script so it didn't take very long, I even added mouse controls. What did take a long time was the period of procrastination between finishing the project and actually adding it to the site. I've been in a procrastinating mood lately, or rather I've not been in a doing things mood. That said I have made progress on Caerostris, I assembled the toolhead.

I beat Terraria with my little brother recently. It was a little anti-climactic because we'd spent a lot of time getting stronger and I'd been using the wiki for build guides. Overall it was a lot of fun. The next game we play is still up in the air, but it's becoming increasingly more likely that it will be Factorio. I'm having my brother play the demo to see if he likes it enough to be worth committing a ton of time to. I worry that Factorio will be annoying to play 1 hour at a time but we'll see. Thinking about Factorio has gotten me to start a new save (which is pretty much always how it goes). This time I decided to try and play as an eco-friendly engineer. This means I try to avoid polluting or killing anything as much as possible. It's been a chill experience so far though I expect that to change when I go to Vulcanus and Gleba.

I went to the library the other day with a list of the five or so books on my to-read list and I only found one of them. However, on my way out I saw some Neal Stephenson books and the name rung a bell so I looked closer and realized he had written Snow Crash. So now I'm reading Snow Crash. It's a really cool book. The world building is certainly wacky but at the same time compelling. This is the book that invented the term "Metaverse", which is how I first heard about it. Despite this the Metaverse has much less prominence in the world building than I expected.

posts.title: 8Vim
posts.content:
Last night I made an implementation of 8Vim for controllers. 8Vim is an alternative android keyboard that I think is really cool. It's based on an old project called 8Pen which is now deprecated. A friend of mine made me aware of it several weeks ago and I was immediately hooked. It feels so much more natural than typing on a mini keyboard with my thumbs. The only issue with it is that it isn't as fast as typing with your thumbs. This is what led me to the idea of using it as an input system for controllers. Typically when you need to type something for a console game it displays a big qwerty keyboard on the screen and you have to slowly move a cursor around it with the joystick to select each key. 8Vim would be faster than the default for this case. And that is why I spent last night making a proof of concept. It's been a long time since I've coded a small, just-for-fun project like this. It feels good. Anyway, it worked great! I think I will put a more polished version of it on this website.

I feel a little out of practice at writing for this blog. I've recently been feeling like I don't really have much to say here, but ultimately this blog is meant to be a record of who I am, so if I have nothing to say I should talk about that. I've been thinking a bit about how I want to change my workflow for this blog. I know that the only routines that will actually stick are daily routines, so maybe I need to write a little bit every day and then make a post using that information every week. There are also a lot of possibilities for using Composable 2DOs to help with this as well. The most important thing is to keep moving. Mind Begets Mind.

Completely unrelated to anything else in this post: I recently found out that putting lotion on my face while it's still wet is way more effective and makes my face feel less greasy all day, major win! I've also been slowly but surely adding better clothes to my wardrobe.

posts.title: Composable 2DOs
posts.content:
When I was in college trying to build out my portfolio, I started a project I called composable todos, which was a to-do list app with the idea that it would have a bunch of optional features that could be added to to-do lists to make them optimized for a wide variety of different applications. I called it composable todos because you could "compose" these different features together to make a list that perfectly suits your needs, and because I wrote it using jetpack Compose. I stopped working on it when I started working as a full time software engineer, but lately I've had more time and energy to focus on projects (as well as a desperate need to organize my time), so I decided to revisit the idea. Rather than work off of the original code, I decided to rebuild it from the ground up in the tech stack that I'm most familiar with, the tech stack I use every day at work: Lightning Server and KiteUI. The main difference with this version is that rather than just make an app I wanted to take advantage of KiteUI's multiplatform stuff and Lightning Server's auto generated deployment scripts and host a server and website that I can use from anywhere. This makes it a lot more useful for organization. So far I've created the most basic form of the app and deployed it.

Caerostris update: the three sections of the toolhead are done, but before I attach it to the printer I need to go back and make sure everything I've done so far lines up with how the formbot kit is meant to be built.

posts.title: Caerostris
posts.content:
I did a lot of work on my new printer, which I've decided to name Caerostris after the Genus of orb weaver spider that makes the biggest webs. So far I've finished the Frame and Gantry, except I realized this weekend after I installed the A and B belts that the kit I bought came with the TAP probe rather than the stock probe and the printed parts for attaching the toolhead to the belts and rails would need to be reprinted. The TAP probe involves mounting the entire toolhead on a small vertical rail and tapping the whole head against the build plate until it hits an optical limit switch. Supposedly it's a lot more accurate than the other probe options so I'm glad to have it and the different parts for it were short prints. The next steps for me are mounting the bed and building the toolhead.

I'm being really good about my routines now, I started using a cleanser on my face every morning and I do a short workout in the evening. I want to keep up both of these for at least a month before I think about making adjustments. I had this idea towards the end of 2025 that in 2026 I would sometimes devote a month towards one particular thing and really focus on that one thing or better myself in that one area. I don't really think like that now. The path to improvement for me is not trying to hyperfocus one thing but to incrementally add and change things in many areas over time. The key concept here is the 80-20 rule, the idea that 80% of the outcome can be accomplished with 20% of the effort. There are small, easy wins to be had basically everywhere, from diet and exercise to fashion to learning new skills. I feel like these days it's easy to get wrapped up in the idea that you have to do something perfect and optimally. Online communities around things like exercise, for instance, are constantly discussing stuff like optimal deload frequency when for most people just going on a walk everyday would increase their life expectancy by a scientifically significant degree. I guess the moral here is "just do stuff", or "don't miss the forest for the trees", or "don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good". Unfortunately no matter how nice those sayings sound, there is no substitute for real understanding.

posts.title: Resident Evil 2 Remake
posts.content:
I often find myself on a Friday afternoon making grand plans for the following weekend. I write a list of all the chores I want to get done, all the projects I want to make progress on. And yet nearly as often I find myself on Monday morning having done none of it. What happened? Where did the time go? This weekend the vast majority of the time went to a game called BitBurner, which is an incremental game that involves writing scripts to interact the world. As you might imagine that sort of game hit me like crack. The rest of my time went to playing the Resident Evil 2 Remake because Abrar really wanted to watch me play it. That was fun, and much more fulfilling than BitBurner because I got to spend time with my friend. As I write this it almost feels like I was asleep all weekend, unaware of the time passing or the things I had planned to do with it. I wish I could go back in time to my past self on Saturday and shake him awake. I would say "Why are you doing this? You have all these things you wanted to do!" I feel strongly that this would work if it were possible. I need to kill BitBurner. I don't have a healthy way to engage in it while also pushing my projects forward. What worries me though is that there exists a craving in me for what BitBurner provides, and I wonder if my projects can possibly provide a suitable replacement. I don't want this to happen again.

The Resident Evil 2 Remake was a very interesting experience. The only survival horror game I'd played before this was Signalis, which is heavily inspired mechanically by the Resident Evil franchise. As mentioned earlier Abrar was watching my playthrough live and I don't think I would have finished it otherwise. I think it's a good game, but I don't like scary games that much. However, there were some parts that I really enjoyed. The level design and lock/key sequencing is very satisfying, and trying to conserve bullets while traversing the zombie-filled corridors is reminiscent of Receiver 2.

posts.title: Voron at T-0 days
posts.content:
The parts for my Voron Trident are set to arrive today. I'm underprepared because I haven't printed any serious ABS parts yet. To that end, this weekend I rooted my 3D printer and began tuning it to print ABS. One of the test prints I did is a series of 30mmx30mmx3mm bricks each printed with a different extrusion multiplier. I printed them in my enclosure, but they all warped. The print still succeeded, but I'm going to need to improve the enclosure's ability to retain heat. I think the main improvements will be sealing the door better and sealing the edges that touch the workbench better. Currently the chamber can maintain 35 C (95 F) while the bed and nozzle are heated for ABS. I will probably need the temp to be over 40 C before I can reliably print ABS. I also finished the YeetHammer this week, which was a lot of fun.

I'm feeling the urge to improve myself more strongly as of late. I want to take that stuff more seriously, especially with regards to my ability to focus. Obviously the way to improve my focus is to train and practice, but focus is much harder to train than a muscle group. "The mind commands the body and is instantly obeyed. The mind commands itself and meets resistance." - St. Augustine of Hippo. In the past I've made changes to my routines or habits all at once and found great success, but this change is not going to work like that. I think it will be a gradual and continuous effort, which is something that I'm not good at. I should read Digital Minimalism.

posts.title: The Yeethammer
posts.content:
This week I printed all of the remaining parts of the Yeethammer and ordered the hardware kit. It's going to take longer than I expected to get the hardware kit so I also ordered the Voron Trident Hardware kit. I haven't looked at the guide to build the Yeethammer yet so I've been having some fun trying to figure out how it all goes together on my own. Spending so much time up close and personal with these parts has given me a real appreciation for how well designed they all are for 3D printing. Parts that press fit together have built-in allowances, none of the parts require support, and I've been able to put together most of it without a guide. It also looks awesome, just holding the unfinished skeleton makes you feel powerful.

One issue I ran into this week was that my parts were warping, I was printing in PLA which is known for not warping so I was a little confused. Warping happens because of uneven cooling, so I tried keeping my apartment hot while printing and it worked. The only problem is that I have a hard time falling asleep when it's too warm, so I also finished building the enclosure I've been planning for printing ABS. ABS is known for warping a lot and it basically requires an enclosed chamber to print in to keep it warm. The printed parts of a Voron require ABS for strength and durability, so I bought some poster board from walmart to make an enclosure.

Random side-note: I hate shopping at walmart, it's too big but always crowded and impossible to find stuff.

I used the poster board enclosure for the last two plates of parts for the Yeethammer and I didn't notice any warping even with a reasonable apartment temperature. I may need to reprint some of the parts that warped before I made the enclosure, but I'm waiting on the hardware kit to arrive before I make that judgement. I'm really proud of the enclosure, even though it's just tape and posterboard.

posts.title: I'm a Project-Pilled Printer-cel
posts.content:
Waiting for my new hotend to arrive was rough. Not being able to work on my projects sucks. One thing that I started thinking about to pass the time was perhaps getting a new 3d printer, one that wouldn't have the issues that my current printer does. I looked at the flagship offerings from the major brands and watched reviews and quickly realized that what I really wanted was a Voron. Voron Design is a group of engineers that design open-source 3D printers. Their goal is to design the best printers that are still accessible to the average consumer. They don't sell these printers, in order to get one you have to source and buy the parts yourself. Voron printers are designed to be highly modifiable which is one of the reasons I want one. Voron is the sort of thing that the 3D printing community was built on and it's inspiring to see it succeed the way it has. I plan on building either a Voron Trident or a Voron 2.4 before beginning the Curta project because either of those printers will vastly outperform my KE in terms of quality and speed. I don't know when exactly I'll start building the new printer but one of the prerequisites is building an enclosure around my KE so that it can print ABS, as the Voron printers have many printed ABS parts.

I installed the new hotend on my printer on Friday and since then it's been off to the races. I finally printed a new deck box and finished the Enigma Puzzle Box (linked in a previous post). Currently I'm working on some organization solutions for my workspace (Gridfinity) and the YeetHammer, which is a 3D printed nerf blaster. I chose the YeetHammer as a project because it looks cool and will give me some experience with projects involving hardware + 3D printed parts, which includes both the Voron and the Curta. I've become somewhat unsatisfied by Cura slicer lately. It works well enough, but it doesn't have support for several features I want like having projects with multiple plates and pausing at layer. The reason I'm not using OrcaSlicer is because I can't get it to run on Linux. I've done a lot of searching for a way to fix this but nothing has worked. Last night on my walk I thought of a solution though: I can run OrcaSlicer on my laptop which is still running Windows. This would make it so I still get to use OrcaSlicer without having to deal with rebooting my PC all the time, plus I finally have a use for my laptop. Another thought I had on this subject is that I could use my laptop to monitor the printer remotely which would also make it safer to leave my printer unattended.

My projects have made me happy, but I've been thinking about the year of aesthetic recently and I find my efforts lacking. Cutting my hair right at the beginning of the year of aesthetic was probably a mistake. I'm starting to understand some of the ways in which my physical appearance affects me mentally, and having long hair made me feel better about myself. So what can I do to fix this? Obviously I can't make my hair grow any faster but there are other ways I can improve my appearance like skincare, working out, and fashion. I want to start putting more effort into these things.

posts.title: I Hate 3D Printing
posts.content:
Ok I don't actually hate 3D printing, but I've experienced a major setback. This Thursday I started a print for several pieces of a puzzle box before leaving for work. When I got home from work, I saw this:

This was very disappointing to say the least. I don't have any footage of the moment that the print failed, but I imagine that one of the imcomplete pieces lost bed adhesion and stuck to the nozzle. As the print continued, new filament from the nozzle further cemented the part to it and the motion of the printhead knocked all the other parts off the bed or stuck them to the nozzle as well. At some point the mass of parts stuck to and jammed in the nozzle overcame the pressure of the extruded filament and the new filament was instead forced back up and around the hotend. It took me a while to clean this up, and ultimately only one part was broken, the silicone sock that goes around the hotend for insulation. The hotend still has PLA residue on it, and while I was looking for a site that would ship replacement parts to the US, I found a hotend upgrade kit for my printer. It claimed to prevent leaking and improve performance, so I went for it. It should get here in about a week, at which point I will go back to loving 3D printing. In the future I'm going to set up a webcam to watch the printer so I can watch it from anywhere and remotely stop a print.

I've been slipping back into old habits as far as sleep and media consumption as of late. I need to strengthen my dedication to these things. I am better than I was yesterday, and I will be better tomorrow than I am today.

posts.title: I Love 3D Printing
posts.content:
I've been doing a lot of 3d printing lately. I have a lot of different potential projects that I want to be able to do so I've been printing a lot of test prints to try to dial in the best settings for my printer. I currently have nine identical prints in front of me, each printed with different settings.

The first thing I tested was using the input shaping calibration. This didn't have any effect, which makes sense since I've done that calibration in the past. The next thing I did was take my printer of the square of foam that it was on. I put the printer on the foam to try to reduce vibration both in prints and my apartment. Removing the foam made for a better test print, so I'm not going to put it back, plus moving my printer is sort of a pain. From there I focused on reducing the speed of the print. At first I reduced the speed of the whole print, then just the speed of the outer wall. One interesting result here is that the ringing actually got worse when I reduced the speed of walls to 50% of what it was. I didn't notice this result at any other speed. My theory is that below a certain speed the 3d printer has enough natural damping to prevent this from happening. While I was printing all these test prints I noticed some minor issues with warping, especially near the corners of the test print. One thing that can cause warping is wet filament, which I thought was impossible because I live in a desert. However, I've had the filament for over a year, and I live in a studio apartment, so I guess it's picked up enough moisture to start behaving poorly. It's not a huge deal yet, but I may invest in a filament dryer at some point in the future. Once I had established a good print speed, I started printing a puzzle box design I found online. This particular puzzle box is neat because it prints in-place, which means no assembly required. I was having some issues getting the first layer to adhere to the bed properly. This was a familiar issue to me with this printer, I dealt with it a lot when printing Hextraction. One trick I discovered recently is that cleaning the bed while it's hot almost always results in the next print failing, so now I take the bed plate of the heating element and let it cool down before cleaning it. I don't really know why this is the case. The cleaning process is just wiping the plate with a microfiber cloth and isopropyl alcohol. The idea is to remove oils, dust, and debris from the surface before printing. One reason this particular print was having trouble with the first layer was that it had multiple parts, which essentially increases the surface area of things that can go wrong. I messed around with a few different settings before finally taking the nuclear option and printing the first layer thick, slow, and hot. This did the trick, and I should have done this earlier because the print was going to take over 24 hours anyway, so a slower first layer didn't make a difference.

I haven't fully fleshed out my thoughts on this, but the whole concept of puzzle boxes is sort of strange to me. They are sort of a cross between a riddle and a toy. I say riddle instead of puzzle because I think there is a valuable distinction to be made between the two. Puzzles give the player all the necessary information they need to find the solution, riddles do not. Puzzles are solved by deduction, riddles are solved by induction. I tend to prefer puzzles over riddles, though there are examples of riddle games that I enjoy like The Roottrees are Dead. When I think about good puzzles I think about video games like Portal Reloaded, Baba is You, Linelith, Taiji, or Bean and Nothingness. These games present the player with a series of puzzles where the player can know all of the elements of the puzzle, as well as all of the rules governing those elements, and still not be able to figure out the solution. The solution logically follows from the information the player knows, and following that line of logic is the challenge of the game. Puzzle boxes, however, typically bear little resemblance to this framework. They often rely on hidden, unintuitive mechanisms designed to test the player's patience rather than their intelligence. The mechanisms themselves are often clever and delightful, but solving the box often leaves those mechanisms hidden from the player. It's sort of like the inverse of a magic trick. A traditional magic trick will perform something that seems impossible, something that shatters reality, but when the secret is revealed it loses it's appeal and becomes mundane. When solving a puzzle box, on the other hand, the player might find some arbitrary hidden move and be unimpressed even though the mechanism enabling that move would blow their mind. Obviously this analysis does not include all puzzle boxes. The series of 'The Room' games tend to be a combination of virtual escape room and virtual puzzle box, and I've found the entries I played to be enjoyable.

posts.title: Relaxation Weekend
posts.content:
I decided this week to focus on relaxing this weekend. I live a pretty chill life, but this week I noticed I was exhibiting some signs of stress so I figured I would attempt to nip it in the bud. I think the source of the stress was my mind being cluttered. I've been pulled in a lot of directions lately by various projects, project ideas, and time commitments to friends and family, so this makes sense. Focusing on relaxing has gone well. I spent my time cleaning my apartment, eating good food, and enjoying some quality media. Tomorrow morning I'm going climbing with my cousins before work so I'm even going to go to bed early tonight.

Several of the projects I want to work on will involve 3d printing, so I started doing some tests and calibration for my 3d printer. The main issue I have with it is ringing which in the 3d printing space refers to ripples in the surface of a print caused by the printer vibrating. I've done some things for this in the past, but now I'm approaching it more scientifically with a test print.

I don't talk about current events much, on this blog or otherwise. In the past I've heard people talk about how spending time on social media increases their anxiety and depression because of all the bad stuff going on in the world and at the time I didn't relate to that. Social media algorithms show people things that they engage with and I tend to not engage with the sort of misery porn that other people seem to. These days however things are bad in a way that hits a lot closer to home. The current administration is using ICE agents to stoke violence in this country and drive us closer to civil war. I don't know what to do about this, if anything. Its getting harder and harder to ignore.

I finally made the decision this weekend to share this blog with my friends and family. I started this blog just for me. I think putting it on the internet made it feel like enough of a commitment that I kept posting. I do worry a little bit that sharing it with specific people like this will influence how I write these posts. But I think at this point I've sort of found my voice so that worry is much less pressing than it was when I first started the blog.

posts.title: This website has existed for 1 year and 3 days
posts.subtitle: ...and all it got was a fresh coat of paint!
posts.content:
I finally finished House of Leaves this week. I was reading it bit by bit every night, and while I'm glad I read it, that was not the optimal way to do so. Reading a little bit every night is great for non-fiction but House of Leaves in particular is meant to be read in a certain way. It's hard to describe what House of Leaves is about. I think thematically it's about confronting the void. Textually it's about a guy assembling a manuscript that some old guy was working on before he died and sort of losing his mind, though that story takes place in the footnotes of the manuscript itself, which is about a film about a house that's bigger on the inside, though notably this film doesn't exist in the world that the manuscript exists in. See what I mean about it being confusing? Many times while reading it I got the sense that I would appreciate it more if I had more of a literary background. This might inspire me to seek out some classic literature, but probably not. I feel I would have to take that on as a sort of project, and at the moment I have plenty to do. I don't want to say too much more about House of Leaves as I think spoilers could really damage the experience, so the last thing I'll say is: go read it.

I've been doing more work on the website this week. This is the main project that's been occupying my time. I made some changes to how the blog system works and I implemented the style processor script. As of writing this I believe something about the style processor script has broken the blog, but I haven't gotten around to investigating yet. The style processor adds to the site theme in ways that css is unable to. Currently that is just adding color to certain parts of text within elements. For instance, certain keywords are given a specific color and text in quotes is colored orange. I'm really happy with how everything turned out and I look forward to filling up some of the empty space that fills most pages at the moment. The home page now looks like this:

A few days ago was the one year anniversary of this site existing. This is longer than I ever really expected to maintain it for. I even joked multiple times in the first blog posts about how I was probably going to abandon this project soon. I even kind of did abandon it for several months during the summer last year. I started this website because I wanted to change and keep a record of myself. I'm a different person than I was a year ago. Not in the pedantic "No man steps in the same river twice" kind of way, but in real, measurable, concrete ways. I am more focused, more capable, and more competent than I was a year ago. I hope I can say that every year.

posts.title: New Website Style!
posts.content:
This week I completely rewrote the website style. On Monday, I pushed a commit to my github repository for this site that cleared out the file containing posts because I believed that that was a better way to organize the site. What I had forgotten was that the repository was several updates out of date with the site and also that I had a github action set up to automatically deploy the site to neocities on every new commit. What this meant is that I lost all updates made to the site since before I finished the blog encryption system. So most of this week was spent recreating that, and the new style was a bonus to make me feel better. I decided to try and recreate the default VSCode color scheme, and I think it turned out really well. I plan on making a script to further process all text on the site to do some advanced theming that can't be done with css. Using only color to distinguish the semantics of various site elements is reminiscent of my note-taking strategy from when I was in school. However, using exclusively color definitely doesn't meet accessibility guideline. Ultimately I'm glad I lost updates because I doubt I would have made these drastic changes to the theme otherwise.

One thing I thought about while making the theme change is that I don't actually have very much content on the website to show the theme off (aside from this blog). To this end I've been doing some thinking about what content I could add to the site. I think the main thing is that I need to put more explanation on the various things that are here.

This weekend I watched all of season one of The Pitt, a medical drama about a team of ER doctors. It's a really great show and I'm looking forward to watching season 2 when it comes out.

posts.title: The Year of Aesthetic
posts.subtitle: Not quite New Years Resolutions
posts.content:
I've decided that my theme for this year is aesthetic. I will be improving my image, putting more effort into how I present myself and my space, and increasing my appreciation of art and style. Some specific projects along this line that are already planned include: a visual overhaul of this site, a visual overhaul of my apartment, rebuilding my hairstyle from the ground up, and continuing to work on my desktop experience. I chose a theme rather than resolutions because I care more about having a direction than specific tasks. I often lose interest in specific tasks, but my overall direction should be maintained. I chose this theme as a continuation of things I started doing and thinking about last year. I want to carve out more of an identity for myself as I realized last year how valuable and important that is.

This past week I got sick at the cousin reunion, but luckily it was after all the planned activities were over. My throat still hurts a bit but I'm otherwise healthy. I went back to my parent's house after the reunion for most of the week. I got to spend a lot of quality time with all my siblings. They are all doing well and that makes me happy to see. My youngest sister was very excited to see me and wanted to play together the whole time I was there. She's 4 years old. I don't remember the ages of my other siblings, but her birthday was just before new years. My new years passed uneventfully because we aren't big party people. While I was there I made a gingerbread house and as a joke I filled it up with pimiento olives. We didn't eat the gingerbread houses while I was there, however, so I didn't get a chance to make a big reveal. I think it's one of the funniest things I did there, so hopefully they figure it out soon. Or at least leave it in the refrigerator.

posts.title: OpenSUSE, Holidays, Sleep
posts.content:
Recently I switched from using Linux Mint to using OpenSUSE. The two reasons I did this are one: rolling release, and two: KDE Plasma. Now that I'm using OpenSUSE, I can confidently say that neither of those reasons have disappointed me. The built-in notes widget isn't compatible with my Cinnamon Desklet, but I was able to recreate the key functionality using the command output widget, which made me feel clever. KDE Plasma widgets also have allowed me to put the Monterey Bay Aquarium Kelp Forest livestream on my desktop, which is very cool. My next addition is going to be a way to easily make and upload blog posts. In conjunction with that I'm committing right now to make a blog post every weekend until the end of January. I want to try that out and see how it goes and I think one month is a proper trial period.

Speaking of trial periods, the novelty effect of my bedtime routine has without a doubt worn off. I'm still following through with it but I've been going to bed a little later and waking up a little tired-er lately. This could just be an effect of the longer work-days, and if so I'd expect this to change in January, but if not then it's something I still need to work on. January is also when my new project committment ends, so I can foresee that being enough of a push in the wrong direction to do some real damage.

Anyway, before that I'm going to Mexico with my cousins and grandparents. I'm excited to see everyone again, the last time we were all in one place was Nauvoo, but that was more of a family reunion, and the cousins that are my age were both on missions (Mormonism). I hope that I'm able to represent myself well and leave a good impression. I've made big progress on defining who I am since then. I've never been big on traveling, and going to Mexico in the Winter seems like it defeats the purpose of Winter, but I'm sure there will be fun stuff to see and do there. I've been completely uninvolved in the planning for this one so I'm going in completely blind. Just now while typing this I solved an issue that's been bugging me with my new OS. I've been noticing that my main monitor is weirdly blurry and games won't recognize it's full resolution. On a whim I changed the display scaling from 150% to 100% and that completely fixed it, though I have to scale up my apps and stuff now.

posts.title: Linux Mint, New Paradigms, Note-Taking
posts.content:
I'm working 9 hour days at work this month so that I can have 2 extra days off around the holidays. So far it's gone well. The hardest part is meals, I have to prepare something early in the morning or have leftovers ready to take to work. I've been supplementing this with candy lately, which is effective but not sustainable. All in all, this makes for a good stress test of my routine.

I checked out House of Leaves from the library yesterday. It's an amazing experience. It's very immersive. I will have more to say but I have only just started and this isn't what I want to talk about in this post.

I installed Linux Mint on my computer and have been using it almost exclusively instead of Windows 11. This transition has occupied the majority of my thoughts lately. Linux Mint comes with the Cinnamon desktop environment by default and that comes with some neat customization features. The one that I have gotten the most mileage out of is Desklets. Desklets are little widgets that live on your desktop. Some of the Desklets I have are the weather forecast, a clock, my family calendar, the latest xkcd, and a notepad. The family calendar widget I made myself using an existing photo frame desklet as a template. The desklets are just javascript, though they use a weird ui framework. I also modified the notes desklet to support limited markdown. I am very proud of what I've done so far, control over my environment is my biggest form of self-expression.

I've been thinking about note-taking lately, in no small part because I have a virtual notepad on my desktop at all times (I even added it to my work laptop by syncing the notes file with syncthing). Notes are a representation of the mind of the note-taker, and I sometimes feel that the linear format of a text document is too limiting for me. House of Leaves does seem to be trying to disprove the 'linear' part of that statement, but it doesn't gain anything in clarity by doing so, which is a requirement for a note-taking framework. Just now I looked through some of my old school notebooks and was reminded of the highly non-linear, somewhat schizophrenic way I used to commit information to paper. I kind of miss that, though it's unclear how much of that feeling is me missing being in school. I don't think physical notebooks would work all that well for me nowadays. After all, nearly my entire life is spent in front of a computer. Back when I had just a laptop it made sense to also have a notebook for writing things down rather than having to frequently switch tabs. Now, however, such a thing doesn't make logistical sense. I will have to make do with what I have. More frequent blog posts when keeping a record is the concern, several digital notepads containing different topics, spreadsheets when applicable. Writing this blog post was cathartic, but choosing to start writing was difficult.

posts.title: A collection of things that I've been doing lately
posts.content:
I started playing ARC Raiders since my last post. I will note that this does not break my commitment because I started playing it so I could play it with Abrar. It's a lot of fun and a very interesting design. I've already spoken about it plenty with Abrar so I don't really feel like rehashing it all here. The main idea is that the possibility of cooperating or attacking the other players leads to a lot of interesting dynamics.

I'm trying out jogging a little every night before bed alongside my normal walking. My plan is to jog two blocks uphill every night for a month or so and then maybe step it up. The reason I'm jogging uphill for only two blocks is so that I'm less likely to develop shin splints, which has happened all of the times I've tried to pick up jogging as an adult. It's sucked so far but if it works and I become able to run a lot consistently it will be well worth it. On the topic of my bedtime routine: I finally finished the Broken Empire trilogy and I liked it so much that I decided to read some more stuff by the same author. So now I'm reading the Red Queen's War trilogy which is set in the same universe. I'm not entirely sure of the timeline yet but it takes place after Jorg's adventures in Gelleth. I think I kind of like being able to just ramble about what I'm up to like this (I'm writing this section last). It feels good to say all this stuff without worrying about how I'm perceived.

A couple weeks ago I was having trouble starting my motorcycle in the morning. The first time this happened I worked from home that day, walked to work the next day and bought a battery charger. This time however I had to get a ride from Justin because my car had expired tags (last time it's battery was also dead). It was very frustrating but I've more or less solved it now. At first I just drove my car to work for a week and had my battery tested at O'Reilly, but they said there was nothing wrong with it. So then I talked to Dan about it (or rather he asked me about it) and he said he'd come over some time and help me debug. He mentioned jumpstarting it which I hadn't tried, so the following weekend I did that with my car. I have to insert a sidenote that I got an email from my landlord on the 15th that starting that night cars parked on the street would be ticketed. This really frustrated me and, I'll admit it, I crashed out a little. Afterwards though I successfully jumpstarted my motorcycle and parked my car at the local grocery store. I also bought a jumpstart pack. I've been riding my motorcycle to work every day since then and I've only had to use the jumpstart pack once. One trick I read online is to open the throttle a little when starting it. I guess this just makes the engine heat up a little faster.

I made chicken tikka masala recently. I made it on a whim because I saw a white nationalist complain about it in response to JacksFilms tweeting "when the fajitas come out sizzlin'". I picked a simple recipe and it turned out really well! It's really interesting how the sauce is based on yogurt rather than a roux or soy sauce, it makes the resulting meal much more filling than I expected. While I was making it I realized I was out of cumin so I had to run to the store to get some more. The store only had tiny containers of cumin! I go through cumin fast because I make taco seasoning a lot so this was very distressing for me. The cumin I had before I ran out was one of those big containers that I think I got from my family when I moved to college. I wonder how long it will take me to use up the rest of the spices I got then. The thought makes me feel oddly melancholy.

posts.title: Warhammer 40K
posts.content:
Recently Abrar challenged me to fight her in Warhammer 40k, so I agreed on the condition that she learn MtG and fight me in that game. That's been a lot of fun. I made a spreadsheet to calculate the probabilities of combat outcomes. To deal damage in combat in 40k you have to roll dice 3-4 times with each time depending on the outcome of the last. This leads to some fairly complex distributions, so I learned a lot of new tools while making the spreadsheet like ARRAYFORMULA and SEQUENCE. I'm very proud of the spreadsheet.

And now for a quick update on my bedtime routine and attention economy interventions. The bedtime routine could not be going better, I am consistently much more rested in the morning and less tired throughout the day. I also have not had any trouble keeping to the routine, though sometimes if it's late or raining I will skip either the walk or the reading. As for the attention economy interventions those have been largely successful. I definitely spend less time on youtube and more time on things I consciously choose and I've had little trouble sticking to the interventions. I could be spending less time on youtube, but this is a good start. I feel a small anxiety about my bedtime routine, either worried that I might not stick to it or worried that it might stop working. I suspect this will go away in time.

posts.title: Content Consumption
posts.content:
I've been working on changing my model of content consumption. My old model is essentially entirely ruled by the algorithm. I am but a content pig being slopped. The new model revolves around removing the youtube feed. The idea is that I will search for specifically the content that I want and will spend less time consuming slop. I've made a few other interventions with the same goal of improving my brain function and ability to focus. I will no longer download books in favor of checking them out at the library. I have set my phone to greyscale, which apparently reduces addictiveness. These are all inspired by Nathan Laundry and his video on Digital Minimalism. I also added a weather and time display to my desktop using Wallpaper Engine. I've switched all my clocks to show 24-hour time and all temperature displays to show Celsius. I'm trying to switch to using these systems instead of or in addition to 12-hour time and Fahrenheit. I joked to Abrar that this was in preparation for the American Century of Humiliation, but I don't really know why. I think I just wanted to feel in control.

The following is something I typed out shortly after watching Nathan Laundry's video while considering the ideas presented. I'm putting it here unedited because I'm lazy and tired.

The main problem here is discoverability, how is one to learn about new creators, new topics, or new temporally relevant videos that aren't relevant otherwise? Ironically I would not have been inspired to consider making these changes if I had not been recommended the video from Nathan Laundry. What other framework changes might I miss out on? I feel like for me it is hard to come up with new ideas and I can only iterate on old ideas. Having a constant flow of novelty could be useful. The solution that Nathan Laundry presents is to have a Standard Operating Procedure of allowing access to the youtube feed for a short time in the morning where you can save the videos you want to watch for later. My patterns of listening to music don't work well with this SOP.

Anyway, I'm feeling hollow and unmotivated again. It's not really a big deal but one of the reasons I started this blog was so that I could look back and find patterns, so I probably ought to keep better track of this. The last time I felt like this was my Birthday, and the upswing happened the day after. I've felt pretty motivated between then and now.

I've started/restarted the bedtime routine of taking a walk and reading a little right before going to sleep. It's worked pretty well but I've been doing it for less than a week, so it could still just be the novelty effect. I started by reading the coffee table book Mad Science by Theodore Gray (the guy that wrote The Elements). However, I got a library card this weekend and checked out King of Thorns. Last night I read that before bed and this morning I got stuck in a half dreaming limbo. I really don't like when that happens, and I think reading too much fantasy right before bed contributed to it, so I'm going to try to avoid that going forward.

posts.content:
Today is my birthday, I am 22 years old. I've been working full time at LK since my last birthday. Life has been feeling a little hollow lately (and I'm not just talking about Silksong *laughtrack*). My mood about this fluctuates back and forth over time, with a period of a month or two. I want to accomplish things. I want to be proud of what I've accomplished in my life. Here are some things that I've accomplished:

  • Beat Silksong with 100% completion
  • Pantheon of Hallownest
  • Celeste Chapter 9
  • Got a real job
  • Got a Motorcycle
As you can see, I have no memory of things that happened over a year ago. I don't feel particularly proud of these things. Perhaps this is because I knew when I set out to do them that I would succeed. Perhaps this is because they happened in the past and feel boring now. Perhaps this is because these challenges didn't take very long. Each of those possibilities is contradicted by at least one of the examples I've given. I yearn for the next challenge, I think it will be a puzzle game of some sort. Something that I can devote myself to with no guarantee of success (unless I cheat). Of course this must be a game from my list of unfinished games or else I will have to wait until 2026 to begin. Something that I think I have left unsaid in my posts on this topic is that starting a challenge, be it game or project or otherwise, and then leaving it unfinished makes me feel really bad about myself. This is why I made the 2026 committment.

Anyway, moving on to the small-talk portion of this post: my birthday. As these things go, I got calls from various family members where they sang Happy Birthday to me and asked me about my life. This reminded me that I am out of practice at holding those sorts of conversations, I need to have random tidbits about my life ready to go before these things happen. That being said, I wasn't really in the optimal mood for that sort of conversation at the time. I do appreciate my family, but I'm feeling anti-social lately. I made brownies and bought ice cream as a half-hearted attempt to do something special. I didn't even realize it was my birthday until my Aunt texted me asking if it was a good time for her to call (it wasn't, I was at work). I hope this post doesn't sound too whiny. posts.title: Friction
posts.content:
I think the fundamental characteristic of modern life is the lack of friction. Everything is easy: food, entertainment, travel, everything in the world has been streamlined to an absurd degree. I'm far from the first person to talk about this, but I think that the best solution is some kind of shift in mindset, which is why everyone talks about it and yet it continues to be a problem (mindset problems can only be solved on your own). One of the tricky parts of this problem is that some reductions in friction are good and some are bad. What makes a reduction in friction good or bad? Let's examine some examples of friction reductions that we know are good or bad and try to find a pattern.

My stove reduces the friction of having to start and maintain fires to cook on. I consider this to be a positive reduction in friction. By having a stove instead of a fireplace, I am safer, and cooking is faster and more convenient. On the other hand, I have very little skill at starting fires and don't get the enjoyment of being near a fire every day.

Fast food is a reduction in friction. It provides highly palatable food at any time quickly, but people lose skill at cooking and control over their diet.

Amazon is a reduction in friction that I consider to be positive. It provides easy access to basically any product but I spend much less time physically shopping.

We have to look a little deeper, the true downsides of reductions in friction are often second- or third-order effects. Essentially the downsides are not the immediate tradeoff but the change in behavior that the tradeoff causes.

Anyway, the reason I started writing this was because I was watching the Angela Collier video about christmas presents and had the thought that algorithms are too frictionless for my health. This idea spun off into some possible plans for ways to intentionally choose the slop I consume rather than be fed it by an algorithm that optimizes for watch time.

If I had a house I would devote each room to a different project. "But what about computer projects?" posts.title: Camping in the Boundary Waters
posts.subtitle: Also Hollow Knight
posts.content:
Last week I went camping with my family in the boundary waters. While I was there I had a lot of time to think, so I'll share some of these thoughts here. First, however, I will explain the conditions of this camping trip. The Boundary Waters is a state park in Minnesota with tight restrictions around how you can camp there in order to keep the area as natural as possible. Every time I've gone camping there I've gotten a lot of mosquito bites, eaten rehydrated food, and slept poorly, and this trip was no exception. So it was in this state of deprivation from modern convenience that I was doing all this thinking. First of all, the deprivation itself seemed to have a positive effect on my mental state, specifically my ability to focus. I had my phone, but there was no signal, so I was limited to reading books and playing Simon Tatham's Puzzles. The other entertainment that I brought with me was a hand-crank powered radio, that I got for christmas last year. This made me want to listen to the radio more in the future and to have building a radio as a project. I also might go camping more as a means of balancing myself. I also want to improve my focus by having less background noise (music, podcasts, etc.)

Silksong came out today! I made a promise to myself to not start any new games this year, but Silksong is the biggest release of the year by far and a game I have personally been waiting for for 5 years. So, I made a smaller promise: I will not play Silksong until I beat The Pantheon of Hallownest in Hollow Knight. Because of the camping trip, I started this challenge only three days before Silksong released, and finally finished it just now. I felt like giving up several times in these past four days, but I'm glad I didn't. I'm proud to have finally followed through on this, and I see it as a sign that I will continue to follow through on future challenges.

posts.title: Wedding, Motorcycle, Dominion, Boundary Waters
posts.content:
This weekend I went to my cousin Todd's wedding. It was a fine experience, it's sort of strange that he's younger than me and getting married (I'm 21 at time of writing). I was mostly there to see my family, play board games, and show off my motorcycle. The wedding and reception were on Saturday, but I went back to play more board games on Sunday. This meant I spent around 4 hours driving my motorcycle this weekend. Over the course of those 4 hours I got increasingly comfortable driving my motorcycle like a motorcycle and not like a car. On the way home on Sunday I was lane splitting a bunch and going as fast as my bike could take me (allegedly).

I brought my dominion expansion (Menagerie) on Sunday, and played one of the presets for it. Playing Magic has changed my perspective on Dominion somewhat, and I decided to build a custom set with the goal of making more interesting games. Looking at dominion cards through the lens of Magic, certain cards seem obviously broken. For the purposes of this post, broken means that if the card is in a set it will dominate the viable strategies to an unhealthy degree. One example of this is Bandit, which builds your economy and attacks your opponents economy for a relatively cheap price. When the Bandit is in the supply, the best defense against it is having Bandits of your own. Another example more broadly is cheap action cards that give you +cards and +actions. These cards have almost no downside to be in your deck, leading the dominant strategy to involve chaining many of these cards together on your turn. The set I built had the goal of avoiding broken cards, fostering strategic diversity, and speeding up the pace of the game both through shortening the average turn and increasing the amount of interaction you do on other player's turns. I haven't tested it yet (I think I will have to go to the next board game night to do so) but I think I did a good job. I will update this post to include the list of cards I picked later tonight when I have time. I also have had the idea kicking around in my head for a while that Silver is underrated in Dominion, I want to test this by making a simulation of Dominion where the players only buy silver and provinces and see how fast the game ends. I could then use this as a baseline to compare to actual games of Dominion.

Next week I am going camping in the Boundary Waters with my family. The past times I've gone to the boundary waters have been broadly positive experiences, so I'm looking forward to it. I'm not looking forward to flying out to Minnesota and back, however. I dislike flying, but not because I'm afraid the plane is going to crash or something, I dislike flying because of the hassle and stress of airports. I lost my favorite jacket at an airport several years ago and I still feel kinda bummed when I think about it.

posts.title: I will not start any new games or projects until 2026
posts.content:
I mentioned in a recent post that I had made the commitment in the title of this post. I made this commitment as I was coming off of my short-lived Space Engineers phase. I made the commitment because I have a long list of games that I have played a lot and enjoyed, but then abandoned in favor of something new. I don't want to be the sort of person who is constantly getting bored of what they have and reaching for something new. I need to prove to myself that I'm not that person. The first game I revisited as part of this commitment was more than a little symbolic of this goal: Celeste. I've played through the main story of Celeste at least four times now. This time around a line that stuck out for me was when Madeline says: "I'm done breaking promises to myself." I empathize deeply with that sentiment. Breaking a promise to oneself can do a lot of damage. The reason Celeste was on my list of unfinished games is because I never beat Chapter 9. Chapter 9 was added to the game as a free dlc many years ago and when it came out I put a fair bit of time into trying to beat it, but ultimately gave up. Actually, "Gave up" isn't quite right, more accurately, I started playing something else and didn't come back. I believe that was the second time I played Celeste, with the first being when the game released. The third time was when I introduced Ben to the game and replayed it alongside him. That time I also had the goal of beating Chapter 9, but I wanted to finish all of the C-sides first and I got stuck on 7C (widely considered to contain the most technically difficult screen in the game). I don't remember what game I left Celeste for that time, but I know that the familiar pattern repeated itself. This time, however, I didn't give up. Once I had beaten all the C-sides I spent the Sunday before last completing Chapter 9. Chapter 9 is titled "Farewell", and when I finished it it certainly felt like a fitting end to my journey with Celeste (similar to my feeling when I beat the true ending of Cave Story), however, lately I've felt a nagging desire to go back and get the moon berry and the golden berries. I think I will go back to it someday, but not until next year.

Anyway, I started CrossCode shortly after finishing Celeste, I'm having fun, though progress is slow. I need to reduce the friction of making blog posts, this will likely involve hosting a server and adding a rich text editor and authentication to the frontend.

posts.title: I Finished the Blog!
posts.subtitle: and it only took 4 months!
posts.content:
I finally finished the blog encryption system so now I can go back to posting here. Will I actually do that? Probably. The main reason I was motivated to finish the encryption system was that I kept having deep thoughts and thinking "I should really write this down".

I'm using the encryption system to encrypt blog posts that I don't feel entirely comfortable sharing publicly. That being said, I intentionally used an encryption method that is possible to crack, so anyone who is dedicated enough to reading the encrypted posts theoretically could. The way it works is that blog posts are stored in a json file as part of the Neocities site and they are retrieved at runtime by the blog page. Only the ciphertext of the encrypted blog posts is stored on the neocities site because all files on the site are publicly accessible. This is why I added an encryption tool to the coding projects page, I will use that tool to encrypt the posts before adding them to the site. I think overall this is a fairly reasonable solution given the requirements I had for it.

Now I'm going to list some other things that have happened in my life since my last post. I've been going climbing with Soren on Wednesdays, I got a motorcycle, I got more into MtG, then less into it, and now I'm more into it again, I've played a bunch of new games, I've interacted with TLGTW a lot more and even hung out a few times, I haven't spoken to Ben in a while, and I made a committment to not start any new games or projects until 2026.

posts.title: Magic: the Gathering
posts.content:
Two weeks ago, I asked Soren to teach me Magic: the Gathering. In response, he invited me to the final day of the CEDH league he was running at a local game store. I was interested in MtG for a few reasons, part of it was that I was looking for solutions to the problem I laid out in a previous post, the other part was probably that I had heard about MtG one too many times on Intentionally Blank. Anyway, I went, and after some minor miscommunications about the time, I played Magic for the first time. When Soren arrived he was tired and busy running and participating in his event, but he did introduce me to some of the regulars. Unsurprisingly, basically everyone there knew him. I played Commander with one of the store managers named Chris and a regular named Brandon who let me borrow one of his decks.

The following Tuesday Soren invited me back for the game store's Magic night. I showed up before him and was able to borrow a deck from someone who's name I forgot and play some more Commander. The game store is packed on Tuesdays, and when Soren arrived he couldn't find a game and had just gotten some wisdom teeth pulled, so he left shortly after arriving. I played a few more games and then bought a preconstructed deck before leaving. I bought the zombie Aetherdrift precon. I've been back twice more since then, both times being a week after one of the previously described instances. I've also been using my 3d printer to make some MtG accessories, I've already printed a life counter and a deck box and I'm planning on printing another that has space for tokens and counters

All in all, this has been a very positive experience. I can see this local game store becoming my "third space". I also enjoy playing Magic, learning the game has been a rewarding experience and I expect it will continue to feel rewarding in the future. The next part I want to try is deckbuilding, but I feel like I want to do that with cards in front of me rather than searching online. I may buy the Foundations Starter Collection to facilitate this. How far will this hobby go? Only time will tell, but a conservative estimate says at least a couple months.

posts.title: The Roottrees are Dead
posts.content:
Lately I've been playing The Roottrees are Dead, a detective game where you put together a family tree using an in-game search engine. It's a lot of fun, I beat the base game last night and I'm going to start the expansion "Roottreemania" when I'm done writing this. The basic game loop is as follows: reading through collected pieces of evidence for keywords to search, searching those keywords, getting more keywords and pieces of evidence. This is fairly simple, but it makes for a rewarding experience. This gameloop makes the game different from other detective games in a few key ways:

  1. Built in difficulty curve. The more pieces of evidence and keywords you find and use to fill out the family tree, the more the search area for new clues expands and the more the number of undiscovered clues diminishes. This can lead to some tedium towards the end but my experience was well balanced enough.
  2. Feeling of player agency. This game empowers the player to self-direct through the game far more than any other detective game that I've played. This is probably also why I cared so much about the story, despite the fact that nothing particularly crazy happens.
The only other thing I have to say about this game for now is that I played it on the recommendation of TLGTW

So I haven't really made any meaningful improvements to this site, but I did start playing the Integrated MC modpack with Ben (and Sofia now). I decided to self-host the server, which was a fun new experience. It's relatively simple all things considered, but it was weirdly difficult to find clear instructions for it, I think as a result of 3rd party hosting services being so popular. The server runs very smoothly for me, but Ben and Sofia were complaining about lag yesterday, so I've lowered the view distance in the server's config file, which should hopefully fix that.

The modpack itself is primarily a combination of Ars Nouveau, Create, and Integrated Structures, with a bunch of tweaks and supporting mods to tie everything together into one (integrated) experience. Overall it feels much more intentionally designed than other modpacks I've played. I'm really excited to get into Ars Nouveau because it has a complex spell system sort of like Noita. Our first few sessions have been primarily resource gathering and base building, but I'm hoping to get started on some more interesting things this session. I just need to finish setting up some basic farms and then we can go to the nether. A bunch of stuff in the create mod is locked behind the nether because they require blaze burners. I love the create mod, it adds to the base game in such a natural way. I think that has to do with how tactile and physical the contraptions are, everything makes intuitive sense because it's based in reality.

I'll probably make several more posts about our progress through this mod, at least as long as we keep playing it. I was somewhat hesitant about starting another minecraft playthrough, but this modpack has me hooked in a way few games ever have. Contrary to things I've said in the past, it seems like there might be some experiences that Minecraft is the best medium for. This merits further exploration, another time.

That's the end of the blog post.

posts.title: Introductions
posts.subtitle: What am I doing here? Why am I doing it?
posts.content:
I've rehearsed in my head what I would write here, but now that I'm doing it, I can't remember any of it. Anyway, welcome to my neocities website and blog! I started to want to do something like this (keep a record of myself) for a while now, and I think neocities is the perfect medium for it. As stated I plan to use this blog to keep a record of myself, and I likely will not share this with anyone. I will also intentionally put very little effort or thought into what I post here, as I want to lower the friction of making posts so that I actually make them. I hope that I keep this up, but the odds are definitely in favor of me abandoning this project sometime in the next few weeks.

Regardless of all that, I will now lay out my plans for the blog with more specificity. I want to make posts about media I consume, things I accomplish, and events in my life, with perhaps a sprinkle of deeper, more personal/philosophical ramblings. These posts should be pretty much stream-of-consciousness, which probably will be awful to read, but should be a more genuine way of expressing myself.

So, what have I been up to lately? This neocities page of course! I worked on the main page yesterday and decided to start today by making this post so that I didn't put off starting indefinitely. I plan on streamlining the process of making these, though how exactly I do that will depend on the limitations of neocities pages and how I end up organizing the blog section of the site. I want to be able to search and sort these posts on the website, so I've considered putting them all in a json document, but that may make images difficult. Alternatively, if neocities allows me to dynamically grab all the files in a folder, I'll use that instead.

I'm not sure exactly what style I'm going for for the site. Currently the main page looks like this:

The background image is the same image from the JWST that I'm using for my work laptop wallpaper. I want the paper in the middle to look like continuous feed computer paper, so hopefully I can learn enough css to make that happen.

That's the end of the blog post.
